title: Edmund and the Atlas
premise: Edmund Dravenmoor works his father's type cases in a border-city print shop as revolution smolders in 1848. When a sealed letter hidden inside an old atlas implicates the Dravenmoors in a forged armistice plot, Edmund must smuggle the incriminating plates past three military checkpoints before the treaty is signed. Betrayed by the family friend who planted the evidence, he chooses truth over loyalty to his father's old allegiances, testifying at the signing and saving both the city's printing quarter and his own conscience — though the shop burns, and with it the family name.
about_author: Tamsin Blackwood is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing nineteenth-century printing ephemera before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted bindery on the coast, where she restores hand presses that no longer work.

chapters.title: The Weight of Lead
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In the print shop's final week before martial law closes the district, Edmund sorts type while his father Gideon burns correspondence he won't explain. The emotional beat is quiet dread: the ordinary rhythms of craft masking a family secret Edmund can feel but not name.

chapters.title: A Letter in the Atlas
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Repairing a water-damaged atlas for a customer, Edmund finds a sealed letter sewn into the binding naming the Dravenmoors as custodians of forged armistice documents. The beat is vertigo — the discovery that his family's obscurity was camouflage, not poverty.

chapters.title: What Father Burned
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Flashback chapter: twenty years earlier, Gideon cut the plates under coercion by Colonel Vasseur, then hid them rather than deliver them. The beat is guilt; we learn the letter is Vasseur reclaiming his leverage now that the war's end makes the forgery valuable again.

chapters.title: Three Checkpoints
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Gideon, ill and frightened, asks Edmund to move the plates to a neutral monastery before the signing. Edmund maps the three checkpoints between shop and sanctuary. The beat is reluctant resolve — a craftsman planning a smuggling route like a page layout.

chapters.title: The First Gate
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, interleaved with a soldier's. Edmund hides the plates inside a delivery of hymnals and passes the first checkpoint through sheer bureaucratic boredom — until the soldier notes his shaking hands. The beat is terror sharpened into competence.

chapters.title: An Old Friend's Offer
chapters.summary: Family friend Aldous Rennick's POV. Rennick, revealed as Vasseur's informant, offers Edmund safe passage in exchange for the plates and silence. The beat is seduction: Rennick genuinely loves the family, making his betrayal more corrosive than any enemy's.

chapters.title: The Second Gate
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At the second checkpoint, a young officer recognizes the hymnal order as impossible — the monastery burned out last month. Edmund talks his way through with a lie about replacement stock, but the officer follows him. The beat is hunted adrenaline.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Ledger
chapters.summary: Gideon's POV. Dying of fever, Gideon confesses everything to Edmund and begs him to burn the plates instead — protecting the men whose names are on them, some now honest officials. The beat is the book's moral crux: loyalty asking Edmund to bury the truth forever.

chapters.title: The Third Gate
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Climax. Cornered at the final checkpoint by Rennick and the pursuing officer, Edmund chooses testimony over escape: he surrenders the plates publicly, naming Vasseur before the assembled signatories. The beat is cathartic rupture — the quiet man finally speaking.

chapters.title: Reset Type
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, epilogue one year later. The forgery trial ends the war honestly; Vasseur falls, Rennick emigrates in disgrace, and Edmund reopens a smaller press under his own name, setting new type over the ashes. The beat is earned peace: inheritance reclaimed as choice, not burden.
